utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Respondents are here. Good morning, everybody. Could you please call the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, appearing for the Prosecution, Joanna Korner, Andrew Cayley, and assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman. I'm assisted by co-counsel Milka Maglov, legal assistant Milos Perec, translator Ratislava Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For General Talic, Michel Pitron and Ms. Natasha Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, as it is common practice here, I will first start with you and ask you whether you are hearing me in a language that you can understand. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Talic, I put the same question to you. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I can hear you well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we proceed any further with Dr. Donia, I want to raise now - because it's becoming apparent that we cannot proceed in this fashion with any efficiency - the question of how we deal with the authenticity of documents. Your Honour may recall that Mr. Ackerman, when I was opening the case, interrupted to tell Your Honours that there was an objection to the authenticity of the document colloquially described as the Variant A and B document, the instructions to the Serbian people. Your Honour may also recall that Mr. Ackerman told Your Honour that in a case that had been conducted in this Tribunal earlier, it was the Prosecution in the form of Grant Niemann, who was then a senior trial attorney, who had objected to the authenticity of the document. Your Honour may recall, when I was opening, I explained that after ten years, witnesses had memory lapses. It would appear that Mr. Ackerman, after six years, may have also had a memory lapse because we actually found with some difficulty the transcript of the actual part. Can I hand Your Honours and Mr. Ackerman a copy thereof? I apologise. It's on -- in e-mail form.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I may be able to shorten this. Just a moment. I spent the entire afternoon yesterday afternoon searching through the Celebici transcript looking for what I had been told a couple of days ago was surely there. It was not. What it actually boils down to is that Mr. Niemann had made objection to documents that did not bear stamps or signatures but did not specifically refer to the Variant A/B document, although it falls in that category.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be one of the problems, as I say, of recalling the events of some years ago. But as you will see, the objection came to the document Variant A and B from Mr. Ackerman in December of 1997. Now, Your Honour, can I deal with --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me again. I'm sorry. I hadn't seen this, Your Honours, before I -- when I spoke. But this is a totally different part of the transcript. The part of the transcript where the issue comes up is the cross-examination by Mr. Niemann of a witness called -- it's either Hadzibegovic or Vegicic [phoen] or something like that. It was during the Defence case. This is during my cross-examination, I think, of Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, perhaps to save --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears that Mr. Ackerman was referring to something completely different, but he raised it in respect of Variant A and B. Your Honours, can I deal with what is going to happen if this objection is maintained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This particular document. But I then want to come on to the general principle. Your Honours, we have this morning given to the Defence counsel the 22 versions that we have accumulated over the course of investigations. This document has figured in virtually in every case that involved a Prosecution of Bosnian Serbs since the Tadic case. We can call, and I will call, an investigator to show exactly where we have received from -- where we have received these copies from. Your Honours, we have just given that also to the Defence counsel. And can I tell Your Honour in brief what this investigator is able to say? He is able to say, for example, that he personally collected from the government of the Republika Srpska the transcript of the speech made by Radovan Karadzic in which he referred to the Variant A and B document and has a statement from the shorthand writer who transcribed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is actually a reference to that part of that speech in Dr. Donia's report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. In addition to that, Your Honour, he can tell the Court where the various documents have come from. One of them, the most recent, was actually collected by SFOR from the SDS offices in February 2000. Your Honour, we can actually go on like this for half a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, Ms. Korner, let me put my cards on the table straight away. You know as much as we do of the best evidence rule. That's the rule that you need to follow. Just make sure that dealing with such an important document you will forward -- you will bring forward the document itself that is available to you. I understand if it existed in the original language and if it has an official stamp on it or whatever, you could bring that. I mean, it's up to you. It shouldn't be as difficult as you would imagine, because I figure -- as I figure it, this is a very important document. If there is an allegation that the document that you are referring to and on which Dr. Donia bases part of his report, then I imagine the Prosecution will base a substantial part of its -- of its case. Then -- I mean for this Tribunal to be convinced of the non-authenticity of the document as against being convinced of the authenticity of the document, it's going to -- it's not going to be as difficult as you would imagine, I mean because this is a cardinal document in the opinion of the Tribunal. I mean, if there is allegation that it is not authentic, we will see. I mean -- well, I would expect from you to bring whatever evidence, and you will have all the space which you need to bring the evidence necessary, and we leave it at that. But I don't think you should worry that much about it at this stage, because I would expect from you to receive the evidence that you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will take -- it will take a lot of effort, if you follow the best evidence rule, for this Tribunal to be convinced that it is not authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what I'm trying to explain to Your Honour is this: Of course we can do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's going to be time-consuming.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's going to be fantastically time-consuming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, but you are faced with that problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm attempting to do at the moment is to see whether we can't foreshorten this. I imagine that Mr. Ackerman - I don't know whether the Defence for General Talic take the same view on this document - must have some sort of instructions before he challenges the authenticity of this document. Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman may wish to reconsider the position, but the situation is this: We cannot, in order, in our submission, to most efficiently conduct the trial stop and start like this in relation to documents that witnesses are going to refer to. It seems to us that the only way to deal with this is to deal with this, as it were, in a chunk when we deal with each witness. Now, in future, we will be providing to the Defence in advance a list of the documents as disclosed that the witnesses will refer to, and we will be asking the Defence to let us know in advance of the witness which documents are objected to as not being authentic or not in some form or other being admissible, and we will then ask Your Honours to make a ruling, there having been a hearing if that is necessary. Because otherwise, what's going to happen is that the witness is going to come in. The Defence will -- we will put a document to them. The Defence will say, "We object." If we don't stop and deal with it there and then, then either the document is not admitted or it is, and it becomes very confusing. I'm so sorry, Your Honour. May I finish explaining what's going to happen otherwise? First, there is this system where you can have documents which are not admitted into evidence or are marked or something like that, but the transcript is going to become impossible to follow while in the middle of a witness's evidence we have an argument about whether the document is admissible or not. Now, in respect of Dr. Donia, Your Honour, I don't know. I did ask yesterday -- we telephoned the Defence yesterday after court and asked if they could provide us with a list of documents to which they objected. In Dr. Donia's evidence we don't know at the moment. But we cannot have Dr. Donia referring to documents, some of which are admitted, some of which are not, because we're going to be asking Your Honours at the end of his evidence to admit into evidence those documents and mark them as admitted, and until we've had the ruling, we can't do it. So, Your Honour, I mean, at the beginning of a trial it's a bit more difficult to foresee what will happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But may I suggest we have two choices at the moment. One is that Dr. Donia can continue with the evidence referring to all the documents that are in the binders that Your Honours have. Because we've started, at the end we will ask for a list of those documents to which the Defence object, and we will then have to have legal rulings from Your Honour so that we can decide what is admitted into evidence and what is not. Alternatively, Your Honours, we can certainly deal with the Variant A and B document today. The investigator is available. The documents have been given to the Defence. They are all more or less the same. They just have different numbers. And we can deal with that straight away, and we can deal with any documents that the Defence object to in Dr. Donia's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a problem that we encountered during the Pre-Trial Conference, and more or less the attitude taken by the Defence was along the lines that you know already. They do not want to disclose at this point in time, or give particulars as to various documents which again potentially cause a lot of problems to this Tribunal in the course of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I will avoid it as much as I can, but I am not in a position at this early stage of the trial to pre-empt the issue because I don't myself know which documents they will be contesting. So I realise that there are problems, but the problems also are of a different nature. For example, yesterday when Dr. Donia started giving evidence, I was given a file, a box file, with I don't know how many documents. Now, neither -- none of us is in a position to know which of these documents are going to be or have their authenticity contested by the Defence. Neither do you. But when were these documents first given to the Defence in any case?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, all these documents, bar I think two or three, were disclosed way back to the Defence. They're all part of the disclosures. They've just been pulled together. But, Your Honour, accepting that the file like that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes a difference. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say I understand this has been raised with a great -- I'm sorry. With the greatest respect, I can't see what the problem is about Your Honour simply saying to Defence counsel -- may I say Mr. Ackerman has already indicated in respect of other documents to which he objects. There is -- there can be no reason at all why counsel for General Talic cannot say, "These are the documents in this particular file which this witness will refer to, to which we object." Unless they do that, Your Honour, we can't continue in any efficient form at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. I don't see it the way you see it, because so far the position taken is that I only know of one, maximum two, documents that we had an indication that their authenticity was being contested until yesterday. That's about it. I have not heard from the Defence that they are contesting all these documents or other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will come to you in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to clarify matters, my learned colleagues representing General Talic have in fact -- this morning we've just had a notification of the documents that they are challenging. It's fairly -- it's a fairly wide-ranging objection. All documents that are not signed or stamped, they will object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That, they have said all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then they have given us a list of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but this they have said all along. This is the position that I'm trying to explain. During the Pre-Trial Conference, you were pre-warned that that would be the position that the Defence for General Talic will be taking. Actually, also Mr. Ackerman for Mr. Brdjanin also gave an indication that certain documents which purportedly emanate or are attributable to his client are not authentic. So concentrate on those, because you were forewarned. I am not in a position now to tell counsel for General Talic or counsel for Mr. Brdjanin, "You have until tomorrow morning to specify exactly which documents." They have said all the documents that bear the signature of General Talic or purportedly are attributable to him, and they were limited only to -- you remember, Ms. Korner, they were limited only within the context of the internationality of the conflict. I mean, all others, yes, I am going to put my foot down and say that you have a time limit. We can't possibly proceed in a vacuum not knowing which documents are going to be contested and which documents are not going to be contested. And there you are 100 per cent right. But there is also a limit, a limit as to what to expect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think we may be at variance on that, because I can't see the difficulty. I understand the general principle. But in other words, that puts the onus on us to search through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You always have the onus.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the onus on us to search through -- we have the onus to prove the case, Your Honour. But the onus on us to search through each of the documents in advance and guess or do the best we can to say these documents, because they're not signed or they're not dated, are the subject of challenge. But they may not be. Some of the documents may be innocuous. I'm sorry. May I finish, Your Honour, because it really is an important principle. For example, when we got under the reciprocal disclosure rule some documents from the Defence on both -- for both defendants, they gave back to us effectively as documents on which they relied documents that come from -- that we've disclosed to them, and they're giving it back to us to show that they're relying on them. These documents all come from the same sources. Some are undated. Some are unsigned. But they rely on them because they're helpful. So how are we to guess, Your Honour, that this is -- this particular unsigned document may not be the subject of dispute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I am not the Prosecutor. You are the Prosecutor, and you represent the Prosecution here, together with Mr. Cayley, et cetera. The onus, the burden of proof, rests upon you. Whenever you file or exhibit a document or whatever it is, you are duty-bound to provide also evidence as to the authenticity of the document. Now, how you do it, that's -- the Tribunal will not interfere. But if you are filing or presenting a document purportedly coming from the state council purportedly signed by General Talic or signed by Mr. Brdjanin, or whatever, it -- you ought to -- you should not only present the document but present also supporting evidence to make it -- at least to show that we are dealing with an authentic document, to start with, and that if it bears a signature of supposedly General Talic, you will have someone to say that that is the signature of General Talic. Now, you also have to anticipate that you may have problems there and, therefore, your first problem and first preoccupation should be to foreclose on that as much as you can. So how you do it, that's your business. But I can't stop the Defence from contesting the authenticity of any of the documents you intend.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely right, Your Honour. Your Honour cannot stop the Defence. They can object. At the end of the day though, Your Honour will have to make a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. And probably not at the end of the day. Probably much before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. By "the end of the day," I didn't mean the end of the trial. Your Honour, may I say Your Honours anticipated rightly for the majority of these documents the Prosecution will be able to say these documents were seized or provided. That's all that we'll be able to say. Occasionally, we can call a witness. For example, Your Honour -- and I raise this now, the document that Mr. Pitron objected to yesterday, the report from the public prosecutor in Teslic. Now, as it turns out, he is a man who was interviewed. We've provided to the Defence the Rule 68 material that came from his interview. But if necessary, I can ask Your Honour to show witness summons. I can have him here to authenticate that document. Your Honour, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, just it's a bit more difficult. That is a rare thing. Most of these documents we can only -- we will only be able to say these documents were seized under search warrant in whichever area or have been provided by other agencies. But Your Honour, we will go through all of that if that's required by the Defence, for whatever time it takes. I return then to my original position: It is -- apart from being difficult to follow, it is also unfair on the witnesses to stop/start. Therefore, in each and every case, as Your Honour declines to make an order that the Defence should give us a list of the particular documents to which they object, then we will go through each of the documents that we know the witnesses will be referring to; we will identify the ones that are unsigned or undated; and then before, Your Honour, before we call the witness, we will call such evidence as we can about where these documents come from; and we'll ask Your Honour to make a ruling. Now, in respect of Dr. Donia, as I say, we haven't actually done the exercise, because I'm afraid to say it never occurred to us, if that's what Your Honour was going to do, that we should have to decide ourselves rather than getting any assistance from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. The Defence should actually take, in my opinion, at least, a more cooperative approach, definitely. It would help the Tribunal much more if an indication is given here and now at least with regard to the documentation that was handed to us yesterday to which Dr. Donia is referring. Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if necessary, the Tribunal will also make a ruling to that effect. However - however - the burden of proof -- that's where you have to start from. You have the burden of proof not only generally but also particularly with regard to each and every document or exhibit that you present us with. You are not -- or the last thing that this Tribunal would expect from you - and I know that it will not happen - is to present a document with no supporting evidence as to the origin of that document. And I'm sure we are not going to have documents like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because otherwise, if you choose that, you are asking for trouble.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can -- for each and every document that we have put in, we can show where that document comes from. And of course, Your Honour, if that's what we're required to do, we will do it. Can I return to the instant problem? I'm sorry, I didn't appreciate -- because before I got on my feet, I didn't understand that Ms. Fauveau had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will hear what the Defence has to say now, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we deal with the instant problem? We will go through the documents with the assistance of the list we have from General Talic's counsel. I don't know that we have a list from Mr. Ackerman, but if we have, we'll go through that as well. We will then ask Your Honour to -- we will call evidence. We can certainly call full evidence on A and B, which we will. And we will call evidence as to where each of the documents that is referred to in his report comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's hear Mr. Pitron first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I see no particular objection to the proposal made by Ms. Korner. I believe like her, that it would be necessary to address the question of authenticity of documents before hearing the witness, rather than after. I just have one question that we need to deal with, and that is to give time to the Defence to declare themselves regarding the authenticity of those particular documents. As you know, we have been given hundreds of thousands of documents, and we need to know for each witness -- will be using the documents -- it will be -- he will be relying on. If we know in advance, then we will have no problem in saying which we contest and which we do not contest. We received yesterday at the beginning of the meeting documents from the Prosecution. We worked all morning. We were unable to comment on the authenticity of the documents at the end of the day. And I believe that it would be normal for us to have a few days in advance the documents the witness will be relying on so that we can properly inform the Prosecution what we believe regarding the authenticity, and this will give the time to the Prosecution to produce evidence in support of authenticity. This has been going on from -- for two and a half years. If we are given appropriate time, reasonable time to study the documents, then we will have no problem in working properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Ackerman, on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the air needs to be cleared a bit regarding all of this. First of all, Ms. Korner, I believe, is an experienced trial advocate. She has been working on this case for over two years. And she would thus have known throughout that process that to get a document into evidence, you must prove its authenticity, you must prove that it is what you say it is, that it is the document that you're contending that it is. And she's known that for her whole career, I'm sure. To now stand before this Chamber and suggest to you that there is something improper about the Defence contesting the authenticity of her documents is, I say to you, disingenuous. She has known from the very beginning that part of her job is to prove the authenticity of her documents. And to say that it's our fault that this has become an issue is just not fair. It's not our fault. It's the law. And it's never my fault when I suggest that the law should be followed, and that's all I'll suggesting here. Now, with regard to the particular documents, I have been supplying Ms. Korner with my views of these documents, whether or not I would waive authenticity. And I've been waiving authenticity with regard to a large number of documents and providing her with that information. If she has paid attention, what she has seen is that I am generally waiving authenticity with regard to any document that would ordinarily have a signature and a stamp and does not. In a place like the former Yugoslavia, it is generally understood that a document is not authentic for any purpose if it doesn't have a stamp and a signature, if it's a document that ordinarily would require that. So it should be no mystery to her if I have not replied with regard to any particular document, that if it is a document that does not have a signature and a stamp, the chances are I will challenge its authenticity. I look at these documents, Your Honours, I have no more idea the providence of these documents than you did when you looked at them yesterday. They are pieces of paper without signature, without stamp, that could have been typed on a typewriter yesterday in The Hague. Now, I know the Prosecutor is not manufacturing documents, but that could have happened. It could have happened two years ago somewhere in Bosnia and been stuck into some records just so that they would be found by the Prosecutor. We don't know. And if the Prosecutor is now telling you that we cannot prove the authenticity of most of these documents and therefore we're going to have a great deal of trouble proving our case, they shouldn't have indicted the case in the first place if they couldn't provide the documents necessary to prove it. It should never have been indicted unless they had the evidence. If they -- if they're trying to base their case on a bunch of documents that can't possibly be authenticated, then we shouldn't be here. They should have done that before they ever indicted these people. Now, I'm willing to work forward on this case on the way that Joanna Korner has suggested, that is, if she will supply me the list far enough in advance for me to conscientiously look at the documents and make decisions about how I feel about their -- their authenticity and let her know whether I'm going to object or not, I think we can work pretty efficiently, because I will not challenge the authenticity of many documents, but some I will. And I reserve the right to do that, and I should. I can't do an adequate job for my client if I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also if I may add, part of the pre-trial process was precisely to clear the terrain in this regard, too, and more or less following the documentation that you filed for the purposes of 65 ter. The question of authenticity did arise. It did arise in very generic terms, if I may say so, which definitely is not exactly what the Prosecution would have preferred, but it's an indication -- it was an indication, an early warning of what you were to expect. So basically I think the best way we can proceed is -- I see a lot of validity in what you have suggested and what you have stated and in what you have suggested, and I think I -- I can also see that the Defence approach is becoming more cooperative in this regard. However, we have to understand each other a little bit better. Mr. Pitron, there is a problem in what you have suggested in the sense that if the Tribunal is satisfied that the documents that we are talking about or that we would be talking about on any given day, in any given circumstance, in the case of any particular witness, have been in your possession for months and months, if not years, and you did not indicate to the Prosecution that you were contesting the authenticity of those documents, then we are going to have problems. Not in that I will not give you all the opportunity to state what you have to state and expect from the Prosecution the proof of authenticity in any case but in the time limit or the time -- time space that you are requesting or asking -- asking for which would necessarily bring the trial to a halt and we will be holding this trial with hiccups more or less. This is what I mean. I mean, if we are satisfied that these documents have -- were in your possession and you could have indicated that you were contesting their authenticity, please don't ask me for time. You indicate that you are contesting the authenticity, so that would put the Prosecution on its guard, and they either prove the authenticity or they don't prove it. You don't have to prove anything, as you know. But don't ask me for time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with all due respect, I have -- remind the Court that over 600.000 documents that we received, two-thirds arrived last June, and throughout, until the end of last year and the beginning of this year, I was still receiving documents, and you are telling me that I have had time. With all due respect, Your Honours, no, I have not had time. I have just had time to try and see what they're about, to have them translated, because they were not translated by the Registry. To tell me now that I had enough time to study them, to assess their authenticity, I am sorry. But in view of the way in which the Prosecution is making me work, I have not had time. On the other hand, two things. First, as soon as I receive those exhibits and as soon as I thought that their authenticity can be contested, I say so very clearly. I will not go back on what I have said. A document that is signed is not in dispute. One that has a stamp also is not contestable in principle. One that doesn't have a signature or a stamp is in dispute. I now would like to know the exact documents that each witness will be using. As soon as the Prosecutor tells me that -- when she told me yesterday at 9.00 in the morning -- I will be able to tell her within eight hours what my opinion is regarding its authenticity or not. I am afraid that I can do no better than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. And that is very reasonable on your part as well. That is very reasonable on your part. This is what I meant. I mean, I did not expect you to come here not knowing which documents a particular witness is going to be asked to refer to, definitely not. But don't -- then don't -- if these documents have been in your possession already, I would -- I would expect you to at least be aware of them. I mean, you have been very clear as to which categories of documents you will be contesting the authenticity of. That has been clear. But you have not been clear with regard to other documents, and they have been in your possession, too. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence were given the list of the documents to which Dr. Donia would be referring to, which were footnoted last week. Your Honour, I don't think it's helpful any more to pursue this. I take the point that from now on, and that's what we intend to do, as I said this morning, at least three days before the witness is called the list will be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour -- but then I would expect, Your Honour, and I think Your Honour now expects that we be told, identify the documents to which objection will be taken. Mr. Ackerman made the point that I was trying to make. In fact, he has not contested the authenticity of some documents which are not signed but clearly, presumably, help his case, and that's the difficulty. Can I come back to Dr. Donia? It seems to me the most efficient way to proceed now is for us to look at the documents to which objection is taken, to call the evidence that we wish to call about that evidence to satisfy Your Honour that they should be admitted, and we may have to have a legal argument about what is authentic for the purposes of this case. In other words, we do not have to call the maker, the signer, of all of these documents. But, Your Honour, I think that's the only thing we can do at the moment. I would ask, Your Honour, we may be able to -- if Your Honour gives us an hour or so, we can go through the documents and then try and work out the best way to call the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I suggest, because to tell you the truth, I didn't want to interfere with the way you started producing Dr. Donia as your expert witness yesterday, and I was taken a bit by surprise by the fact that you made available a number of documents which had not yet been exhibited in court. In other words, it's a practice which more or less I don't like. I mean, I would rather prefer to have the documents exhibited, formally exhibited first, any problem as to authenticity cleared, so any question as to admissibility cleared, and then we'll proceed with the evidence. I think it's wiser. It pays dividends to the Prosecution and to the Defence, and although it may delay having a witness come here to give evidence by a day or two, I can assure you that it will simplify matters because then there will be no further questions as to authenticity in the course of the testimony. So if you can take my suggestion. I was going to suggest it yesterday when he started giving evidence, but then I realised that there was no problems with the Defence or forthcoming from the Defence for these documents to be exhibited later and questions as to authenticity discussed, debated, and decided upon later, and so I said let's go ahead. But I would prefer it the other way round, as I have just suggested, if that is agreeable to you. And it would also give the Defence more time to clarify its position with -- their position with regard to these -- to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, you and I are ad idem on that. That's what I said to you this morning first thing. This is the only way to deal with it. Your Honour, I had intended next week, when Dr. Donia had finished, to call the chief investigator in this case to explain the provenance of the majority of the document collections, as we've been calling them, and to deal with how we acquired other documents. It seems to me now that I will have to interpose him before we go any further with Dr. Donia because with some of the documents, they come from these collections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. If we trash today and conclude all the problems that there may be on the documents that Dr. Donia will be referring to, then we can proceed with Dr. Donia's evidence. I will give you this hour that you require.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: See which other witnesses you need to produce and then we'll take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- sorry. The majority of the documents which are not open source documents, in other words, newspaper articles or books that have been written about this, are documents that Dr. Donia looked at from the in-house collection of documents that we have. We will now need to go through them, having got the list of the documents which the Defence object to, in order to establish to Your Honour's satisfaction where they come from. We will have to call that investigator. Somebody's got to give evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is he present?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's here, but I'll have to -- he's certainly not expecting to give evidence today. But I can call and I will call, because may I say that the Variant A and B document affects a number of trials in this building, and I think that the quickest way - and it will help the other trials - is for us to deal with this in full today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for a moment and seek to clarify this from the Defence. Mr. Ackerman, do you still contest the authenticity of the document re: the Variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, and there is -- that same issue, as Ms. Korner has alluded, is in process in a case that's being handled by your colleague Judge Mumba, the Bosanski Samac case. They are litigating that vigorously I see from the transcripts. And we were just handed this morning the Prosecutor's Office's collection of these Variant A/B documents. They have some, I think, 21 different versions of them with different numbers, and many of them have handwriting on them which is in a language that I can't read. We've just had them for a very few minutes, and I don't know -- have no idea whether that handwriting would affect my view of the authenticity of these documents or not. I think there should be an opportunity for us to at least spend some time. My co-counsel will be able to read this, at least spend some time going through it because it may -- it may clear up the whole thing. It may not, but it may. It has that potential. If not, then I think what Ms. Korner suggests is probably sensible, and that is that she go forward and offer whatever proof she can regarding the authenticity of these documents and then the Court can simply make a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Pitron, are you of the same opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like Ms. Fauveau to respond, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We contest this document because the chain of custody was interrupted at a certain point in time, we believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So more or less I would start from there, Ms. Korner. Please concentrate on it, because obviously it forms a -- not exactly the backbone, but almost, of most of the theories or opinions of Dr. Donia, in any case. I would imagine that it's going to be referred to and re-referred to in the course of the presentation of your case by various witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Probably not, Your Honour, but nonetheless, as Your Honour says rightly, it's really the backbone not only of this case but of the Samac case and other cases that this was -- the "blueprint" perhaps is putting it too high but the basis for how matters proceeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let me make myself clear. If this document is so important, then I would suggest to you and to Defence that we start with it before we proceed with Dr. Donia's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to ask, would Your Honour stand Dr. Donia down, in other words, until we've sorted the question of these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. May I have -- he's hardly started in chief. May we have permission to talk to him? We understand after cross-examination starts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is your reaction to this, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have absolutely no objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pitron? Okay. You can go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, would Your Honour adjourn for one hour? As I understand -- is Mr. Ackerman prepared to go ahead? I will call the investigator, Mr. O'Donnell, to deal with -- I'm sorry. Yes. Your Honour, there may be a slight problem. I know it's time wasting, but it can't be helped today, I'm afraid. Would Your Honour say two hours? There's a problem with getting the investigator here within the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. His presence is needed, definitely, and also these two hours will be used by both sides to deal with this. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Incidentally, while we are at this and before we break for two hours, may I raise some points on which I require some clarification. Now, I'm going back to or I refer you to the four motions filed by Mr. -- remaining four motions filed by Mr. Ackerman last week, each one dealing with the first four witnesses after the investigator that you intended to bring forward. As I understood the position to be at the end of last Monday's Pre-Trial Conference, you were exchanging documents with Mr. Ackerman, and we were supposed to make an assessment of -- reassessment of the position at some later point in time with a view to seeing whether these motions were going to be maintained or whether they were going to be withdrawn or at what particular time they needed to be decided upon. Could you inform the Court as to the current situation?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether they're withdrawn, but the current situation is that Mr. Ackerman's have been redisclosed, the documents that he said he didn't have, to him. So I don't know what the situation is. The first witness, in fact, is going to be so far back now. We've already -- he was supposed to be arriving this weekend. We've already put him off until Tuesday, and it seems to me he may not be giving evidence until the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If these four witnesses will be giving evidence, say, within the next two weeks, you need to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is why -- this is why I'm insisting on some sort of information. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, by -- I don't -- I know I've received some additional documentation from the Prosecutor that would take care of some of the documents that I had told you in the motions that I did not have. I think there are still some translations outstanding. I did receive a couple of translations for the first witness. I haven't even compared them with what's missing, I've been doing too many other things, but I think by Monday morning I can tell you what the status of the documents are on those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may very well be they've given me everything I needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it may be that we will call upon you again Monday to possibly conclude this matter. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- sorry, Mr. Cayley just said something about all the other documents that were disputed. But I understand that we've now got a list from counsel of General Talic of all the documents that are disputed in Dr. Donia's report. I'm not sure about Mr. Ackerman, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I sent a message to Ms. Korner late yesterday with regard to that, setting out that as a general matter with regard to the Donia documents, I was contesting authenticity of anything that failed to have a signature and a stamp. I can possibly be more precise about that sometime within the next hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say that in respect -- I have just remembered. I was reminded yesterday by a member of my team that there are still some translations awaited for the first witness. But we were told by the CLSS that they would be available today. And as soon as we get them, we will give them to Mr. Ackerman and to my learned friends. We will also try -- if there really becomes a point where the translation is not available, then we will try and get it translated by not authorised translators; in other words, they're not properly -- I don't think "authentic" is quite the way I want to put it. But that they may not be the proper authorised translations, but they'll be the best we can get them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then there is another matter that I wanted to raise. You are aware that Defence counsel for General Talic filed earlier on this week or last week, end of last week, an objection with regard to 92 bis, et cetera. You had requested the Court for permission to make oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to raise that this morning, because I don't think I made myself entirely clear. We would like to make oral submissions to Your Honour on the witness, Ludwig Kranjc, who is dead. And they object, and I think we need to make submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No need for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. On the other ones, Your Honour, we have nothing further to add, and we were going to ask Your Honour for a ruling because obviously we need to know whether to warn the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I brought it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when would you like the make the oral response with regard to the dead witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can do that at any time that's convenient, because there's no question about having to warn him either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the last point I wanted to raise was -- well, first to your request last time for a possible subpoena --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to the journalist that was mentioned. There was some objection raised at the time by Mr. Ackerman subject to his reconsidering his position after reading the alleged --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was a newspaper article, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- newspaper article. Have you been through the newspaper article, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm very embarrassed. I told you I would do it, and I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you possibly do that by Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That will be another one of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this: I appeal to you to be as courteous with each other as possible. I mean, you will understand that the Prosecution needs to know what they have to do in good time, too. I mean, please try to come with a definitive answer by Monday. So the sitting is suspended for two hours. We will resume at noon. Thank you. And if there are any problems in the meantime, please let me know through the registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm so sorry to have not been in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, that's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was getting some last-minute instructions. It appears, which we hadn't appreciated because nobody thought we were going to have to deal with this quite so quickly, that some of the copies of this particular document have original writing in it, in other words, not photocopy. I'm sorry to ask Your Honour, could Your Honour give us another 20 minutes just so that the investigator is able to specify which have original writing? I'm very sorry that Your Honour has had to come into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These things happen, Ms. Korner. I've been a Judge for the last 25 years. Nothing surprises me any more. If you need more than 25 minutes, please let me know. This is why I had told you before if there are problems, come back to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to have got last-minute instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem. What we are -- the time that we are using now, I can assure you, is being very well made use of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And may I just tell Your Honours that what you have in front of you in the bundle is you have effectively a summary of what the investigator will say plus, in addition, the various copies of this particular document that have been referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think what we will do is I will take this new file with me to my Chambers and have a look at the documents there, and we will resume at exactly half past noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Half past twelve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Half past twelve. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I tell Your Honours, I'll ask to be brought to Your Honours -- in the investigator's, the summary of what he will say, he refers to supporting material, in other words, where that document is referred to. We've copied that, and we'll have that brought out to Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we will resume at half past twelve.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Now, the mike is on. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour for the time, and we are now in a position to proceed. May I mention one matter? Because we were in a hurry to give the Defence documents, entirely my fault, I gave them some documents with what are internal information sheets belonging to the Office of the Prosecutor. I understand that they may have written on them. I'm just simply going to ask that if they feel they can't hand them back to us, they would undertake to destroy them, because they're not -- they're internal communications, effectively. Your Honour, I'm sorry, I forgot to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because Mr. Ackerman wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will return the documents, those cover pages that she's concerned about. Unfortunately, I'd used the numbers on them for notes that I was making. The one thing I wanted to say to the Chamber is having had an opportunity to review the documents that were provided this morning regarding this particular exhibit, this Variant A/B, we have become convinced that there is sufficient circumstantial guarantees of trustworthiness that it is -- would simply be a waste, from our standpoint, of this Court's time to go through this exercise of having this witness come in and spend the next who knows how long testifying as to what these documents say. So at this point, I am prepared to waive my objection to the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pitron.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that my colleague's comment concerns one document that was provided to you and not all documents, and I agree with him with regard to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understood you, you were referring to the Variant A/B document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's my understanding that that was the issue that we're getting ready to spend a lot of time on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. You are not extending your non-objection to the other documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. Ms. Korner has a list of the other Donia documents that I am objecting to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Pitron, with regard to the Variant A/B document, you take the same position?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that changes a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it perhaps might have been courteous if we had been told about this in advance. The fact is that we've now wasted the best part of a morning putting this together. Your Honour, if we have to go through this exercise for every document, this trial will take five years. I think we need to argue quite soon the principles of admissibility into evidence in this Tribunal. Your Honour, what I -- in this case, there's nothing else we can deal with today. Dr. Donia has gone. The investigator who will deal with the other documents that the objection has been taken will be testifying on Monday. He needs to gather together the documents. Your Honour, may I say, however, that we supplied to the Defence last week the full list of the Dr. Donia documents. We gave them -- we recopied for them the first, as it were, set of them. But there are another 15 or so that haven't yet been recopied. As I say, the list has been with the Defence since last week. We would therefore ask that by the end of today, they indicate which of the documents not yet recopied for them they also object to. Can I say, they've all been disclosed some time ago. So we need to know those. And on Monday morning, we will deal with those. And then I would ask Your Honours to hear legal argument on the general principles of admissibility of documents in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think with regard to the admissibility of documents, I think what you suggested this morning and what more or less we agreed upon this morning is the way we should proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I understand, and we will deal with each document -- each set, as it were, each witness. But I think Your Honours need to set out a series of general principles first. Admissibility in this Tribunal has not been historically with the strict proof that may be required in other jurisdictions because of the way that the Tribunal was established and the way in which documents are acquired. I think it is important that Your Honours should look at the decisions that have been made in other cases which we are going to pull together for Your Honours to see. If those very strict principles that Your Honour dealt with this morning were adhered to, I can say without, I think, fear of contradiction, no documents would ever have been admitted and a lot of people wouldn't have been tried here. So I think, Your Honour, we need to look at the general principles and then apply them in turn to each of the witnesses or each of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To some extent, Your Honour, I wish I could have told you yesterday that I would be taking this position, but these documents were handed to me not very long ago. I had to go through them, my co-counsel had to go through them, and about two minutes before this hearing started, we had agreed that we could -- we could now concede that there are circumstantial guarantees of trustworthiness that would, we think, make it possible for the Tribunal to admit this document. If Ms. Korner wants to speed things up with regard to the rest of the Donia documents, all she has to do is give us documents or information she has that she believes established the same kind of circumstantial guarantees of trustworthiness regarding the other documents that are not signed and do not have stamps on them, and if she gives that to us and we're satisfied that it would be a waste of your time, and folly to contest any further those documents, then we will of course do the same thing we did with regard to this document. So it's not that we are dragging our feet about this. It's that if she gives us the information, you'll -- she'll get the response that she would like, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I must tell Your Honour that the bundle of documents that Mr. Ackerman refers to that I was going to hand Your Honour, all of these -- nearly all of those have already been disclosed. If Mr. Ackerman or anybody else had read through the bundles headed "Kljuc," they would have seen the Crisis Staff document that refers to Variant A and B. Krupa, the same thing. These are all documents that have been disclosed. We are not supposed to do the job of the Defence. We say, "These documents are admissible. These are the reasons why." If they wish to challenge them, then they should do the research themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The principle, actually, and I definitely am not going to put the question of authenticity before considering whether these documents ought to be admitted in the first place because it's a question of relevance that comes after. It's a question of authenticity which comes after. These are points that need to be decided once the document is an exhibit. First it has to become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To which there's no question about that. And this is why I was surprised yesterday when Dr. Donia took the witness stand and started referring to documents which were not yet exhibits, because basically you were running the risk then of having those documents not admitted in the first place and having a witness at the same time making reference, specific reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we take the view that if it is known that a witness is going to deal with various documents, unless there is an objection taken, then those documents will be admitted through the witness. But, Your Honour, I take your -- I take the point that Your Honour has made and, as I said, we'll do it differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's why I let it go yesterday, precisely because of what you've said just now and because there was no opposition forthcoming from the Defence, but certainly that's not the system that I prefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think we were more or less on the same wavelength today with regard to the procedure that ought to be followed. And I can tell you beforehand that I'm not going to waste time going into questions of authenticity and decide whether a document is authentic before deciding on whether the document ought to be admitted as evidence or not. Then the question of authenticity has a bearing on the probative value of the document but not on whether -- a priori whether the document should be admitted or not. Otherwise, as you said, we would never start, and we would never finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Korner seems to keep trying to shift her burden to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- and it's not our burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't take it as that. I even think that you were a little bit touchy upon the subject. She was not throwing at you any accusations that you were dragging your feet or whatever. Leave it at that. The Tribunal is quite happy with the attitude that you and Mr. Pitron are taking so far, so there is absolutely no criticism being levelled in your direction for the moment, at least, let's put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to say that is of no value to what we are trying to do for Ms. Korner to say somewhere in the, I don't know, 250.000, 300.000 pages of documents that we have we could have found these. That's probably true if we had had the time to go into that kind of an inquiry. And it's so simple. If she has documents which she believes show that a document is authentic, just let us know. Even give us the numbers. We don't mind looking them up ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I think we are wasting our time here discussing this any further, because as I understand it, there is a commitment on the part of the Prosecution now that a few days before a witness, you will have the documentation. So the question of going through your hundreds of thousands of pages to locate this or that particular document does not arise any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree. The Prosecution has the key to solve the problem, and I'll assist in any way I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not going to -- we did as an exception for Dr. Donia because it was footnotes. We are not going to recopy documents we have already disclosed. We are going to provide the list of the numbers. I don't know how many Amazonian rain forests we've cut down already in this case, but there has to come a stop. But the numbers of the documents will be supplied at least three days in advance of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't expecting you to give them again the copies of the documents. They would complain that they have to read them again. So -- and also --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you looking at me when you said that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you already fell twice from your bicycle. One other thing, Ms. Korner. I mean, I was going through these documents in my Chambers, the ones in Cyrillic script, and again, I mean it's -- I'm saying this from experience. Most of them, apart from the fact that I don't read Cyrillic, but those of them are very poor quality photocopy, and even for an expert in the language it would be very difficult to read or to understand. I mean, they are barely legible. I'm saying this not by way of criticism because I realise that this is not done capriciously. In order to avoid problems, because I can anticipate Mr. Pitron or Mr. Ackerman looking at document so-and-so and saying, "We can't read this. Apart from being in Cyrillic script, we can't read it," and even with the help of interpreters or whatever, that could create problem. So if you can avoid that, it would avoid incidents in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the quality of those documents, I was going to explain to Your Honour, is because of the quality of the copy we have. Some of these are copies, and that is how the document when we acquired it was copied. But we appreciate that. It has happened before where we've had to try and get a better copy. But we're well aware of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because what I mean, for example -- take the document at Tab 12. If you look at it, you tell me whether there is anyone on earth capable of making heads or tails of what the first page contains, or supposed to say, the second page. The third page is not bad. And you continue, there are pages which are utterly illegible. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's because -- I can show Your Honour what I call the original. The original is like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The original is like that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The original is like that. That's why it's come out like this. It's not the photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no solution, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But for some of these documents, I'm afraid, that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So do we have anything else to clear up this morning? Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, nothing, I'm afraid, that we're in a position ready to deal with this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And will you put your request again so that we can formalise it and then I make -- give a ruling on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In respect of the documents, Your Honour, what we're asking for now, please, is the that the remainder of the documents, which we will give them copies of on this one occasion, but could we know which one of those are objected to as well, particularly as chain of custody up here has been raised. The investigator will need to make investigations over the weekend as to how we've acquired all these documents. So I would like the numbers of the remaining documents on the list which are objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand it, Ms. Korner, the chain of custody interruption that was mentioned by Ms. Fauveau related to the Variant A and B document only. I don't think you were referring or making that applicable as well to the other documents, were you?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was referring to -- I was referring to the documents Variant A and B. But I'm not sure that I won't raise this objection again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, that brings that particular matter to an end. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to the balance of the Donia documents, Your Honour, let me just say that I will have no objection as to the authenticity of any document that bears a signature and a stamp and will have with regard to any document that does not. And if this afternoon, as I go through the documents, I find a document that does not have a signature and a stamp that I for some other reason believe is authentic, I will advise Ms. Korner. But absent that advice, that should be sufficient information for her to proceed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that is a commitment on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as it is a commitment, I will not give any ruling, as far as you and your client is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pitron.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say the same -- make the same remark, as I have always done. I am very sensitive to this position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not quite so simple, because on the list that we were given by the Defence, they're objecting to one with a signature on it. Because I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Pitron. It was Ms. Fauveau with respect to one of my team. They object to a document marked 1120, which is signed. Because as I understand it, General Talic doesn't know who the signature is. So I'm not sure that's at all relevant to its admissibility, but nonetheless, it's not so simple to simply say anything that isn't signed or sealed is objected to. So if there are other documents with a signature, then we'd better know about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which document is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the one in Your Honours' binders marked behind or on top of - I'm not sure - one -- I can't at the moment -- I'm sorry, that's the disclosure number, so I'd --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. This is a draft translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The original is signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The original is signed? And this is being -- it's behind -- just behind Tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's a document from a voluntary unit that we have, and it's a document that we received two days ago, so we should look into it. And in addition, this document, it's true, has been signed. But as said -- but as we said to the Prosecutor which document we were contesting, we said that there was an additional document, and we provided the reasons for which we were contesting its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, this document is over and above the declaration that they have made. Please keep in mind that there is, however, this document which does not fall within that description. It goes outside that description. And -- but this will be the only document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that. And I'm not going to repeat this again, but with the greatest of respect, I cannot see why the Defence having had this list for well over a week now cannot simply say, "We dispute documents 1, 6, 9, and 12." It makes it easier for us. We're going to have to do the work to establish it; we understand that. But to not make an order that they very simply give the numbers, I simply do not understand that, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can make the order. So the Chamber orders the Defence for General Talic and for Mr. Brdjanin to indicate -- or to communicate to the Prosecutor via the normal channels - I don't know which channels you use between you, but via the normal channels - which of the several documents contained in the folder of documents to be made use of by witness -- expert witness Dr. Donia they have reservations about or wish to contest the authenticity of by not later than the end of -- You have special times here which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge. Microphone, please, for the President. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So by 4.00 today. And it shouldn't be difficult for anything, but usually there is a time limit which is observed in this Tribunal for either the filing of motions -- 4.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is 4.00. So we'll keep it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, just so there's no confusion, it's on the list that was given to them last week, it just indicate -- we've already got some indications, but just the remainder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The remainder. Yes. Okay. That's taken to be like -- as just stated by Ms. Korner. And in actual fact, that's the way it has to be. So I think we can call it a day for today. I'm sorry this had to happen. But anyway, we haven't wasted the morning as much as you think. It's a useful exercise, and I think it will help us eliminate similar problems in the future. We will resume on Monday, 9.00 in the morning sharp, with the understanding that the investigator will be produced as the first witness, to be -- Do you envisage that he will finish?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know -- at the moment, the objections are so obscure as to leave me wondering what is happening. So I shall wait to see what the cross-examination is and how much further we have to go. Your Honour, I hope that he would certainly finish and that we can deal with the legal argument, if there is to be any, on the principles on which documents are going to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that's -- that would be a -- that we ought not break today with Ms. Korner feeling like the objections are so obscure. I think they're not the least bit obscure. I think the objections we're making are very simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In your case, let's put it like this: I mean, I was prepared, as I stated earlier, not even to address a ruling in your regard. The problem is that I realise that sometimes we face a situation whereby what's clear is not as clear as it appears to be. One instance is this other document which was -- which came to the surface, which does not strictly speaking fall within the description of the reservations or the parameters of the reservations that your colleague had indicated earlier. That is bound to create some confusion within the ranks of the Prosecution, and I have to be fair. I mean, please do take into consideration that our exercise, our function here, to balance the respective rights is not easy. And I have to make sure that if the Prosecution is coming to -- here prepared on Monday producing one particular witness, they ought to be put in a position whereby they know exactly what that witness is going to be produced for and not be exposed to having surprises thrown at them at 9.00 in the morning or at any other given time during the proceedings. That, I will not allow. This is why I have all along stated also that everyone will be asked to bear the consequences of his or her actions. I mean, please do understand that. I am very appreciative when someone like you takes the approach that you have taken, because that is helpful to the Prosecution, and that's how it should be. But if you come on Monday morning saying, "Okay, but in addition, there was another document," that's -- we can't go on like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have a suggestion for another order, Your Honour, which -- my fear at this point is that we're going to walk in here Monday morning and the Prosecution's going to hand us a stack of paper this big that says, "Here are the documents that the witness will use to establish the authenticity of the ones you've objected to." It would be really helpful if the Court were to enter an order that any material of that nature be provided to us by Saturday at 5.00, because then we'd be in a position to walk in here Monday morning and say, "We no longer have objection to documents, you know, 7, 8, 9, 11, 17, 28."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen, Mr. Ackerman, I could have adopted a completely different system which is sometimes adopted in trials in many jurisdictions, many countries. I could have given a ruling to the Prosecution to start the trial by bringing forward all the documentation. That would be precisely the first thing to be done. That could have thrown you into a disastrous confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you ought to be appreciative of the approach that is being taken by the Prosecution. I understand that the Prosecution is coming forward with the documentation batch after batch after batch, because in a trial like this which is going to last months, if not -- if not years - hopefully not - I mean, that's the only reasonable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- sensible way of approaching it. But I think that as we go along, we will find other ways of sorting out these difficulties. However, you ought to understand one very fundamental fact which will always weaken your position, and that is that all these documents have been disclosed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And therefore, you can come forward and say, "But we're talking about hundreds of thousands of pages, et cetera." I mean, I can be very strict, and I can say, "Mr. Ackerman, you have no right to do any other work except dedicate all your time to this case because this is a case, and I will not want to hear anything about the rest of your commitments, rest of your work, and whatever." The same I could say to Mr. Pitron. I don't want to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Therefore, what I expect is that one is always or tries always to be very sensible and reasonable in his or her approach. This is fundamentally important. Otherwise, I will have to put my foot down, me and my colleagues, because the fact remains that these documents have been in your possession, some admittedly since June, but if we're talking from June until now, we're talking of seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have again obviously failed to make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you haven't. You have been very clear. You are appealing to Ms. Korner to hand you these documents by Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
