utterances.text: No. No. No. That's not what I'm asking for. Today when it became clear that we were going to have to have the investigator come to testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, about the Variant A and B document. The Prosecutor then gathered together documents which were handed to the Court and the Defence which caused us to be able to say, "We no longer contest that." Now, if that -- that's inevitably going to be the case on Monday morning. When we come in Monday morning, the Prosecutor will say, "Here is the stack of documents that we have gathered together that we intend to use to have this witness establish the authenticity of documents." All I'm saying is this: If the Prosecutor gathers those documents together, as she inevitably will, to be able to use on Monday morning, it would probably shorten the matter dramatically if sometime over the weekend she would either give us the document numbers so we can pull them out of our own collection of documents, of if they're documents she has not previously disclosed to us, disclose them to us because I would like to walk in here Monday morning, Your Honour, and say, "I no longer have objection to 90 per cent of these documents." That would shorten things up. I'm trying to just do something that will let us move forward on this matter rather than take up more time with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just point out that exactly what Mr. Ackerman has said is the problem. It is not, in our submission, good enough for the Defence simply to say, "If it's not signed, if it's not dated, it is per se, unless you prove otherwise, not admissible."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No reason has been given other than, "It's not signed, it's not dated, so you must establish why it's not authentic." With the greatest of respect, I do not agree. The basis of objection to the admissibility of a document must be something more than that. As to -- as Your Honour has rightly pointed out, its authenticity or its weight, that's another matter. But for it to be admissible in evidence, simply to say, "No signature, no date; we object. You gather together every document," as we have today, "that shows that this" -- we really couldn't do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are a hundred per cent right, and this is how this Tribunal definitely looks at it. One ought to -- and I want to make this very clear. I am not prepared to put either questions of authenticity or questions of relevance at the very premise of whether these documents ought to be admitted or not. Relevance is something that will be decided there and then when we are discussing the document, but maybe also afterwards, because what might appear to be irrelevant at one point might result to be very relevant later on in view of the evidence or testimony of someone else. So basically you can rest assured not to expect this Tribunal to rule a document inadmissible a priori because someone alleges that it is not relevant. Relevance will be seen later on. Questions as to authenticity, what the Tribunal will require, if there is an allegation that that particular document might not be authentic or notice that that -- the authenticity of that document is being contested, then what the Tribunal requires a priori is someone to confirm with solemn declaration that this is a document which he made available or which he recovered or she recovered, et cetera. That is enough for having that particular document admitted in the trial, and then we'll move from then onwards. I mean, the authenticity comes later. If there is an allegation, that I want to know what the allegation is. I want to know if there is any substantive -- any substance behind the allegation or whether it's just being thrown into your court to make your life difficult or just fishing for some sort of future good luck. I mean, let's be practical about it. We will deal with the legal aspects of admissibility on Monday. I don't think there are great difficulties ahead. You know what the Rules are. You also, both of you, you know you are bound by the rule of best evidence as well, and that has a reflection. I mean, if someone tells me that there is an original and you try to file a copy, I'm going to ask for the original, and we'll move from then onwards. I mean, more or less these are rules that are common to all jurisdictions. We must not confuse issues. We must not confuse relevance with admissibility. We must not confuse authenticity with admissibility. We must not confuse voluntariness with admissibility. It's also where we may have differences dealing with lawyers coming from different jurisdictions as to whether certain issues are a matter of fact or a matter of law, but more or less past that, there shouldn't be any big problems. But we will deal with the question of admissibility on Monday. In the meantime, be prepared with your investigator in case we need his evidence. And I would suppose also that Dr. Donia should be informed that his presence may be needed at any given moment, because what happened today could happen on Monday, and you may well be faced with a go ahead from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Donia will certainly be back here on Monday and available if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that clear enough for everyone? We can therefore adjourn. We will resume Monday morning at 9.00, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of January, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
